lessons.title: The ABB flow lineup and when to lead with it
lessons.keyPoints:
ABB Measurement & Analytics makes flowmeters for liquids, gases and steam, plus pressure, temperature, level, positioners and flow computers.
Electromagnetic (mag): ProcessMaster for process industries and AquaMaster for water distribution. Conductive liquids only.
Coriolis: CoriolisMaster measures mass flow and density directly. Best for high accuracy, batching and non-conductive liquids.
Vortex and swirl: VortexMaster and SwirlMaster for steam, gases and clean low-viscosity liquids. SwirlMaster needs very little straight pipe.
Thermal mass: SensyMaster measures the mass flow of gases directly, with no pressure or temperature compensation needed.
Flow computers: ABB Totalflow (for example the µFLO G5 and XFC G5) for natural gas measurement in oil and gas.
Lead with ABB when the customer needs flow on a new project, is replacing an old meter, or has a problem (accuracy, maintenance, straight-run space) the current meter isn't solving.
Most ABB meters share a common operating concept: similar menus, clear text displays and setup through the glass, so plants that standardize on ABB train once.

quiz.q: A customer needs to measure vegetable oil (not conductive). Which ABB family is the natural fit?
quiz.why: Mag meters need a conductive liquid. Coriolis measures mass flow of almost any liquid, including oils.

quiz.q: Which ABB family measures the mass flow of gases directly, without pressure and temperature compensation?
quiz.why: Thermal mass meters like SensyMaster measure gas mass flow directly.

quiz.q: A plant wants to measure steam but only has a few pipe diameters of straight run. Which ABB meter was designed for that?
quiz.why: SwirlMaster needs much shorter inlet and outlet runs than a typical vortex meter.

quiz.q: Why does ABB's common operating concept matter to a plant?
options: It makes meters cheaper to ship
It removes the need for calibration
It only applies to Coriolis meters
Technicians learn one menu style across many ABB devices
quiz.why: Similar menus and setup across devices means less training and fewer setup mistakes.

lessons.title: Magmeters: ProcessMaster and AquaMaster
lessons.keyPoints:
Mag meters measure the flow of conductive liquids: water, wastewater, slurries, acids, caustics. They have no moving parts and no obstruction in the pipe.
They do NOT work on non-conductive liquids like oils, hydrocarbons, solvents or very pure (deionized) water.
ProcessMaster is ABB's process-industry mag: chemical, power, oil and gas, pulp and paper, metals. It offers a very broad choice of liners, electrodes and sizes.
ProcessMaster FEP300 is the cost-effective standard version with quick delivery. Higher-end versions add more diagnostics and options.
AquaMaster is built for water distribution: billing, district metered areas (DMA) and leak detection, including remote sites. Battery and solar power options mean it can go where there's no power.
AquaMaster4 can combine flow measurement, pressure monitoring and data logging in one unit.
ABB also has hygienic mags (HygienicMaster) for food and beverage and heavy-duty mags for tough slurries.
Liner and electrode choice is the key spec: ask what the fluid is, its temperature, and whether it's abrasive or corrosive.
Always ask: line size, fluid, normal and max flow, pressure and temperature, output (4-20 mA, HART, pulse), power available, and hazardous area.

quiz.q: Which of these can a magmeter NOT measure?
quiz.why: Diesel isn't conductive, so a mag meter won't read it.

quiz.q: A water utility needs a meter at a remote site with no power for billing and leak detection. Which ABB mag fits?
quiz.why: AquaMaster is designed for water distribution and can run on battery or solar power.

quiz.q: For a mag meter on an abrasive slurry, which spec matters most to get right?
quiz.why: Liner and electrodes are wetted by the fluid. The wrong choice wears out or corrodes fast.

quiz.q: What's one big advantage of a mag meter in the pipe?
options: It needs no straight run at all
No moving parts and no obstruction, so almost no pressure loss
quiz.why: Mag meters have an open bore with nothing in the flow path.

lessons.title: CoriolisMaster: mass flow and density
lessons.keyPoints:
Coriolis meters measure mass flow directly, plus density and temperature, from one device. Works on almost any liquid and many gases.
Choose Coriolis for: high-accuracy batching and filling, non-conductive liquids (oils, solvents), custody transfer, and recipes where density or concentration matters.
CoriolisMaster FCB400 is the standard design. FCH400 is the hygienic design (EHEDG, FDA-compliant materials) for food, beverage and pharma.
The 430 models are the standard-accuracy versions. The 450 models are higher accuracy (down to about 0.1% of mass flow for liquids) and handle higher process temperatures.
Built-in software packages: FillMass controls a filling valve directly; DensiMass calculates concentration (for example sugar or alcohol) from density.
VeriMass checks the meter's health in place, without removing it, so customers can stretch maintenance and calibration intervals.
Up to five configurable inputs and outputs, so one meter can replace extra devices.
The usual objection is price. Answer with what it replaces: separate density meters, flow computers, product giveaway from inaccurate batching, and maintenance on meters with moving parts.

quiz.q: What three things can a Coriolis meter measure from one device?
quiz.why: Coriolis measures mass flow directly and also gives density and temperature.

quiz.q: Which CoriolisMaster model is the hygienic design for food and pharma?
quiz.why: FCH400 is the hygienic version. FCB400 is the standard design.

quiz.q: A beverage plant wants to know sugar concentration (Brix) as it flows. Which CoriolisMaster feature helps?
quiz.why: DensiMass calculates concentration from the measured density.

quiz.q: A customer says Coriolis is too expensive. What's the best response?
options: Agree and quote the cheapest meter
Show what it replaces: separate density meters, batching giveaway and maintenance
quiz.why: Sell the total value. One Coriolis can replace several devices and cut product loss.

lessons.title: VortexMaster and SwirlMaster: steam, gas and liquids
lessons.keyPoints:
Vortex and swirl meters measure volume flow of steam, gases and clean, low-viscosity liquids. They're a go-to for steam.
With a built-in temperature sensor (RTD) they can calculate saturated steam mass flow without a separate flow computer.
The 450 versions (FSV450, FSS450) add flow-computer functions: they can take an external pressure, temperature or density signal and calculate mass and energy flow, including steam energy.
VortexMaster FSV430/450: flanged and wafer designs. Accuracy about ±0.65% of rate for liquids and ±0.9% for gas and steam. Needs a typical vortex straight run upstream and downstream.
SwirlMaster FSS430/450: about ±0.5% of rate. Its big advantage is short straight runs: about 3 pipe diameters in and 1 out after an elbow or reducer, and about 5 in after a control valve.
Lead with SwirlMaster when space is tight, in retrofits, or when the only spot is right after an elbow. It can save up to 75% of the straight pipe a vortex would need.
Communication options include 4-20 mA with HART, Modbus, and Ethernet-APL on newer models.
Ask: steam (saturated or superheated?), gas or liquid; line size; pressure and temperature; flow range; available straight run; and whether they want volume, mass or energy.

quiz.q: A plant needs a steam meter right after an elbow with almost no straight pipe. Which meter do you lead with?
quiz.why: SwirlMaster needs only about 3 diameters in and 1 out after an elbow.

quiz.q: What do the 450 versions add over the 430 versions?
options: Flow-computer functions: external inputs and mass/energy calculation
quiz.why: FSV450 and FSS450 can take outside signals and calculate mass and energy flow.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good fit for a vortex or swirl meter?
options: Saturated steam to a heat exchanger
Very low flow of a viscous oil
quiz.why: Vortex and swirl meters are a top choice for steam. Slurries and viscous fluids are poor fits.

quiz.q: A customer asks for steam 'energy' to bill a department. What do you need to ask about?
options: Steam type, pressure and temperature, and whether condensate returns
quiz.why: Energy calculations depend on steam conditions and whether condensate is returned.

lessons.title: SensyMaster: thermal mass flow for gases
lessons.keyPoints:
Thermal mass meters measure gas flow by how much a heated sensor is cooled by the gas. That gives mass flow directly.
No pressure or temperature compensation is needed, which keeps the install simple and cheap.
SensyMaster handles many gases: air, nitrogen, oxygen, CO2, natural gas, biogas, hydrogen, argon, helium, propane and more.
Wide turndown (up to about 1:150), so it reads accurately at very low flows. That's great for leak detection and compressed-air audits.
FMT430 is the standard version. FMT450 adds higher accuracy, process-gas calibration, higher temperatures and an ApplicationSelector to switch between gases or setups on site.
Comes as wafer pipe components for smaller lines and weld-on adapters for large ducts and pipes. Very low pressure loss.
SensyMaster FMT400 has SIL 2 certification, so it can be used in safety instrumented systems.
Common wins: compressed air usage and leaks, fuel gas and combustion air to burners and boilers, nitrogen blanketing, biogas.
Not for liquids or steam. Ask about gas type and composition, line size, pressure, temperature and flow range.

quiz.q: What does a thermal mass meter measure?
quiz.why: Thermal mass meters measure gas mass flow directly.

quiz.q: A plant wants to find leaks and track compressed air use by department. Good ABB fit?
quiz.why: Wide turndown and direct mass flow make thermal meters ideal for compressed air audits.

quiz.q: Which model adds process-gas calibration and on-site switching between gases?
quiz.why: FMT450 adds the ApplicationSelector and process-gas calibration.

quiz.q: Which application is NOT a fit for SensyMaster?
quiz.why: SensyMaster is for gases. Water needs a mag or another liquid meter.

lessons.title: Totalflow flow computers for oil and gas
lessons.keyPoints:
Flow computers take signals from a primary meter (orifice, turbine, ultrasonic, Coriolis) and calculate corrected gas or liquid volumes to industry standards.
ABB Totalflow flow computers are widely used in natural gas production, gathering and transmission.
The µFLO G5 (microFLO) is a basic single-run gas flow computer with a built-in multivariable sensor (DP, static pressure and temperature).
The XFC G5 is the extendable flow computer for more runs, more I/O and newer communications (such as MQTT, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth).
They calculate to AGA and API standards (for example AGA 3 for orifice meters and AGA 8 for gas properties), which matters for custody transfer.
They're built for remote, unpowered sites, with battery and solar charging options.
Ask: gas or liquid; primary meter type; single or multiple runs; custody transfer or check metering; power at the site; and how data gets back (radio, cellular, SCADA).
Pair them with ABB pressure transmitters and the right primary meter for a complete package.

quiz.q: What does a flow computer do?
options: Replaces the need for any meter
Takes meter signals and calculates corrected volumes to industry standards
quiz.why: It works with a primary meter and applies the correct calculations, like AGA standards.

quiz.q: Which Totalflow model is the basic single-run gas flow computer?
quiz.why: The µFLO G5 is the basic single-run unit with a built-in multivariable sensor.

quiz.q: Why do power options matter for flow computers?
options: Wellsites and remote stations often have no power, so battery and solar are needed
quiz.why: Many gas measurement sites are remote and unpowered.

quiz.q: Which standard family is used for natural gas flow calculations?
quiz.why: AGA reports (like AGA 3 and AGA 8) cover gas measurement calculations.

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: picking the right ABB flowmeter
lessons.keyPoints:
Start with the fluid. Liquid, gas or steam? Conductive or not? Clean, dirty or slurry?
Conductive liquid (water, wastewater, slurry, acids): mag. ProcessMaster for process plants, AquaMaster for water distribution.
Non-conductive liquid, or you need the highest accuracy, density or batching: CoriolisMaster (FCH400 if hygienic).
Steam: VortexMaster, or SwirlMaster if straight run is short. Use the 450 versions for mass or energy.
Gas at low or medium pressure where you want mass flow (air, natural gas, nitrogen): SensyMaster thermal.
Natural gas custody or production measurement: Totalflow flow computer with the right primary meter.
Then check the details: line size, flow range (min and max), pressure, temperature, accuracy needed, output and communications, power, hazardous area, and straight run available.
If two technologies could work, ask what matters most: price, accuracy, maintenance, or space. That usually decides it.
Not sure? Gather the application data and bring in the ABB rep or inside sales tech support before quoting.

quiz.q: What's the first question when picking a flowmeter?
options: What's the fluid, and is it liquid, gas or steam?
quiz.why: The fluid narrows the choice of technology right away.

quiz.q: Wastewater in a 12-inch line. Which ABB family?
quiz.why: Wastewater is conductive and dirty: a mag meter is the classic choice.

quiz.q: Compressed air to a production line, mass flow wanted. Which ABB family?
quiz.why: Thermal mass meters measure gas mass flow directly.

quiz.q: Two technologies could work. What do you ask?
options: What matters most: price, accuracy, maintenance or space
quiz.why: The customer's priority usually decides between workable options.

lessons.title: Battle card: magmeters
lessons.keyPoints:
Who you'll run into: Endress+Hauser Promag, Emerson Rosemount 8700 series, Krohne Optiflux, Yokogawa ADMAG, Siemens Sitrans F M.
Ask first: what do they have now, how long has it been in service, and are they happy with it? Don't knock the incumbent. Find the pain.
Where ABB tends to win: water and wastewater (AquaMaster for remote, battery-powered and billing sites), a very broad choice of liners and electrodes on ProcessMaster, and quick-ship standard models like the FEP300.
Common operating concept: if the plant already has other ABB devices, ABB mags use familiar menus.
Retrofit angle: ABB designs newer mags to be compatible with previous-generation ABB meters, which makes upgrades easier at plants with older ABB installs.
Pain points to listen for: liner wear on slurries, coated electrodes, no power at a remote site, long lead times, hard-to-use setup.
Don't compete on spec sheet decimals. Compete on fit, service, lead time and ease of use.
Always confirm current specs, pricing and lead times with ABB or inside sales before you promise anything.

quiz.q: A customer loves their current mag brand. Best first move?
options: Ask what's working and what's not, and find a pain point
quiz.why: Find a real problem before you pitch. Knocking the incumbent backfires.

quiz.q: Where does ABB's AquaMaster give you a strong angle?
options: Remote water sites with no power, billing and leak detection
quiz.why: AquaMaster is built for water distribution and can run on battery or solar.

quiz.q: What should you compete on instead of tiny spec-sheet differences?
options: Fit, service, lead time and ease of use
quiz.why: Those are what plants actually feel day to day.

quiz.q: Before promising a lead time on an ABB mag, you should:
options: Confirm with ABB or inside sales
quiz.why: Lead times change. Always confirm before you commit.

lessons.title: Battle card: Coriolis
lessons.keyPoints:
Who you'll run into: Emerson Micro Motion (the best-known Coriolis brand), Endress+Hauser Promass, Krohne Optimass, Yokogawa Rotamass, Siemens Sitrans FC.
Micro Motion is often the default spec. Don't fight the name. Ask whether they need that level of meter on every line, and where ABB's value fits.
Where ABB tends to win: built-in application software (FillMass for filling, DensiMass for concentration), VeriMass in-place verification, up to five I/Os, and a compact, light design with low pressure loss.
Hygienic angle: FCH400 for food, beverage and pharma with EHEDG and FDA-compliant materials.
Value story: one CoriolisMaster can replace a separate density meter, a batch controller or flow computer, and the cost of product giveaway.
Questions that open doors: How do you verify your meters today? How much product do you give away per batch? Do you measure concentration separately?
If the spec says a specific brand 'or equal', ask the engineer what features matter. That's your opening.
Confirm current specs and pricing with ABB before comparing numbers.

quiz.q: Which Coriolis brand is most often the default spec?
quiz.why: Micro Motion is the best-known Coriolis brand, so expect it as the incumbent.

quiz.q: Which ABB features make a strong value story on Coriolis?
quiz.why: Built-in filling, concentration and verification can replace extra devices and work.

quiz.q: The spec says 'Brand X or equal.' What do you do?
options: Ask the engineer which features matter, and show how ABB meets them
quiz.why: 'Or equal' is an invitation to show equivalence on the features that matter.

quiz.q: Which question can open a Coriolis conversation?
options: How many parking spaces do you have?
Do you like your current rep?
How much product do you give away per batch?
quiz.why: Giveaway is real money. Better accuracy pays for the meter.

lessons.title: Battle card: vortex and swirl
lessons.keyPoints:
Who you'll run into: Emerson Rosemount 8800 vortex, Endress+Hauser Prowirl, Yokogawa digitalYEWFLO, Krohne Optiswirl.
ABB's unique card is SwirlMaster: about 3 diameters in and 1 out after an elbow or reducer. Many competitors' vortex meters need far more straight pipe.
Retrofit win: when there's no room for a long straight run, SwirlMaster can go in without re-piping. Re-piping cost often dwarfs the meter price.
Steam win: FSV450 and FSS450 calculate steam mass and energy internally, so customers can skip a separate flow computer.
Questions to ask: Where exactly will it go? How much straight pipe is there? Are you measuring steam for billing or energy savings?
Walk the line with the customer if you can. Seeing the piping often reveals the straight-run problem that ABB solves.
Don't promise straight-run numbers from memory. Check the installation guide or ABB for the exact requirement for that layout.

quiz.q: What's ABB's strongest card against other vortex meters?
quiz.why: SwirlMaster can go where long straight runs aren't available.

quiz.q: Why can SwirlMaster win even if the meter costs more?
options: It avoids the cost of re-piping for straight run
quiz.why: Re-piping labor and downtime can cost more than the meter.

quiz.q: A customer wants steam energy for department billing without a separate flow computer. Lead with:
quiz.why: The 450 versions calculate steam mass and energy internally.

quiz.q: Where do you get the exact straight-run requirement for a layout?
options: From the ABB installation guide or ABB support
quiz.why: Always check the official installation requirements.

lessons.title: Handling common objections
lessons.keyPoints:
'We're a [competitor] plant.' Respect it. Ask what they'd change if they could. Offer ABB for one tough application as a trial, not a full switch.
'Your price is higher.' Ask 'compared to what?' Then compare total cost: installation, straight run, extra devices, maintenance, downtime and lead time.
'We've never used ABB.' Point to ABB's size and history in flow, and offer references, a demo unit or a site visit with the ABB rep.
'Lead time is too long.' Check stock and quick-ship models first. Never guess. If it's long, offer a plan: partial ship, temporary solution or alternate model.
'Our engineer specified another brand.' Ask if the spec allows 'or equal.' Get the engineer the data that shows ABB meets the requirements.
'Send me a quote and I'll look at it.' Before you hang up, confirm the application details, the decision date and who else is involved.
Use the formula: listen fully, repeat the concern back, ask a question, then answer with one clear point.
Never trash a competitor. It makes the customer defend their past choice.

quiz.q: 'Your price is higher.' Best first response?
options: Ask 'compared to what?' and look at total cost
quiz.why: Understand what they're comparing, then show total cost of ownership.

quiz.q: 'We're an Emerson plant.' Good approach?
options: Offer ABB on one tough application as a trial
quiz.why: A small trial on a problem application is a realistic first win.

quiz.q: What's the objection-handling formula from this lesson?
options: Listen, repeat it back, ask a question, answer with one clear point
quiz.why: Listening and clarifying first makes your answer land.

quiz.q: Why should you never trash a competitor?
options: It makes the customer defend their past choice
quiz.why: Knocking what they bought makes them dig in.

lessons.title: ABB pressure and temperature
lessons.keyPoints:
ABB 266 pressure transmitters: gauge, absolute, differential and multivariable models, with base accuracy from about ±0.025% to ±0.06%.
'Through the glass' setup lets technicians configure the 266 without opening the cover, even in hazardous areas.
266 multivariable transmitters measure differential pressure, static pressure and temperature at once. That's ideal for DP flow (orifice, wedge) and compensated gas or steam flow.
266 models are available with remote diaphragm seals for hot, dirty, sanitary or corrosive service, and with NACE options for sour service.
ABB temperature transmitters: TTH300 (head mount) and TTF300 (field mount) accept RTDs or thermocouples, with two inputs for sensor backup and drift monitoring.
SIL-capable options exist for safety systems on both pressure and temperature.
Cross-sell: every flowmeter, pump and tank usually has pressure and temperature points nearby. Ask about them.

quiz.q: What's special about ABB 266 'through the glass' setup?
options: Techs can configure it without opening the cover
quiz.why: Setup through the glass means no cover removal, even in hazardous areas.

quiz.q: Which 266 type helps with DP flow by measuring DP, static pressure and temperature at once?
quiz.why: Multivariable transmitters measure all three for compensated flow.

quiz.q: Why do TTH300/TTF300 have two sensor inputs?
options: Backup if one sensor fails, and drift monitoring
quiz.why: Dual inputs give redundancy and help catch sensor drift.

quiz.q: For a hot, sticky or corrosive process, what option protects a 266 transmitter?
quiz.why: Diaphragm seals isolate the transmitter from harsh process fluids.

lessons.title: ABB level and positioners
lessons.keyPoints:
Guided wave radar (LWT series): continuous level and interface on liquids and solids. ABB's LevelExpert software reduces manual setup like echo mapping.
LLT100 laser level: non-contact level for harsh environments and solids like aggregates, grain and sumps, where a narrow beam helps.
Magnetostrictive level (LMT100/LMT200): very precise level and interface measurement for tank gauging and inventory.
Positioners: TZIDC is ABB's digital positioner for pneumatic linear and rotary valves, with auto-adjust setup and HART. EDP300 is another digital option.
A positioner makes a control valve go exactly where the control system tells it. Old pneumatic positioners are a common upgrade.
Cross-sell: tanks feeding a flowmeter need level. Control valves after a flowmeter need positioners.
Ask: tank height, contents (liquid, foam, solids, interface), temperature and pressure, and hazardous area. For valves: actuator type, signal and communication.

quiz.q: Which ABB level technology fits precise tank inventory and interface measurement?
quiz.why: Magnetostrictive transmitters are very precise for level and interface.

quiz.q: A quarry needs non-contact level on stone in a bin. Which ABB product fits?
quiz.why: The laser's narrow beam works well on solids in harsh conditions.

quiz.q: What does a positioner do?
options: Moves a control valve to exactly the position the control system asks for
quiz.why: It makes the valve follow the control signal precisely.

quiz.q: Which is ABB's digital valve positioner?
quiz.why: TZIDC is ABB's digital positioner for pneumatic valves.

lessons.title: What else to quote with a flowmeter
lessons.keyPoints:
Every flowmeter sits in a system. Ask about the rest of it before you send the quote.
Pressure: a 266 transmitter on the line (pump discharge, header pressure, or for compensation on gas and steam).
Temperature: a TTH300 or TTF300 with a sensor and thermowell, especially for steam, gas or energy calculations.
Control: if the flow is controlled, there's a control valve. Ask about the positioner (TZIDC).
Level: if the flow fills or drains a tank, ask how they measure the tank level.
Installation items: flanges, gaskets, grounding rings (mags), cable, mounting kits, and calibration certificates.
Services: startup help, verification, and spare electronics for critical meters.
Easy question to use every time: 'What else is on that line that's giving you trouble?'

quiz.q: A customer is buying a steam vortex meter for energy. What else should you ask about?
options: A pressure transmitter and temperature sensor for compensation
quiz.why: Steam energy needs good pressure and temperature data.

quiz.q: A customer is quoting a mag on a line that feeds a control valve. What do you ask about?
quiz.why: A controlled flow means a control valve, and often a positioner upgrade.

quiz.q: Which is an installation item for mag meters?
quiz.why: Grounding rings help mags read accurately on lined or plastic pipe.

quiz.q: What's the easy cross-sell question to use every time?
options: What else is on that line that's giving you trouble?
quiz.why: It opens the door to related products without a hard sell.

lessons.title: Units and conversions you'll hear every day
lessons.keyPoints:
Pressure: psi (pounds per square inch) is most common in the US. 1 bar is about 14.5 psi. 1 psi is about 27.7 inches of water column (in. w.c.).
psig is pressure above atmosphere (what a normal gauge reads). psia is absolute pressure, measured from a perfect vacuum. psid is differential pressure between two points.
Low pressures (HVAC, filters, draft) are often in inches of water column. Vacuum is often in inches of mercury (in. Hg).
Temperature: °F = (°C × 1.8) + 32. Water boils at 212°F (100°C) at sea level.
Liquid flow: gpm (gallons per minute) is common. Gas flow: SCFM (standard cubic feet per minute). Steam: lb/hr (pounds per hour).
Mass flow (lb/hr, kg/h) doesn't change with pressure and temperature. Volume flow does, which is why gas and steam often need compensation.
Pipe sizes are nominal: a '2-inch' pipe isn't exactly 2 inches inside. Always ask for line size and schedule if it matters.
Always confirm units with the customer. A psi vs bar mix-up can mean a gauge that pegs or reads in the bottom 5% of the dial.

quiz.q: About how many psi is 1 bar?
quiz.why: 1 bar is about 14.5 psi.

quiz.q: What's the difference between psig and psia?
options: psig is above atmosphere; psia is from a perfect vacuum
quiz.why: Gauge pressure is relative to atmosphere; absolute starts at zero vacuum.

quiz.q: Steam flow is most often given in:
quiz.why: Steam is usually measured in pounds per hour.

quiz.q: Why do gas and steam flowmeters often need pressure and temperature compensation?
options: Gas and steam volume changes with pressure and temperature
quiz.why: Compensation converts actual volume to mass or standard volume.

lessons.title: 4-20 mA, HART and digital communication
lessons.keyPoints:
4-20 mA is the standard analog signal: 4 mA = 0% of range, 20 mA = 100%. 12 mA = 50%.
Starting at 4 instead of 0 is a 'live zero.' If the signal drops to 0 mA, the control system knows the wire is broken, not that the reading is zero.
Two-wire (loop-powered) transmitters get their power from the same two wires that carry the signal.
HART adds a digital signal on top of 4-20 mA. It lets technicians configure the device and read diagnostics without new wiring.
Fieldbus protocols (FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA) carry fully digital data for many devices on one cable.
Modbus is common for connecting to PLCs, SCADA and building systems.
Ethernet-APL is the newest option: Ethernet all the way to field devices, including hazardous areas. Some new ABB flowmeters support it.
Always ask what the control system needs: 4-20 mA only, HART, a fieldbus, Modbus, pulse outputs, or Ethernet-APL. The wrong output means a return.

quiz.q: A 0-100 psi transmitter outputs 12 mA. What's the pressure?
quiz.why: 12 mA is halfway between 4 and 20, so it's 50% of range.

quiz.q: Why does the signal start at 4 mA instead of 0?
options: So a broken wire (0 mA) can be told apart from a zero reading
quiz.why: That's the 'live zero.'

quiz.q: What does HART add to a 4-20 mA signal?
options: A digital signal for setup and diagnostics on the same wires
quiz.why: HART rides on top of the analog signal.

quiz.q: What should you always confirm before quoting a transmitter or flowmeter?
options: What output or communication the control system needs
quiz.why: The wrong output or protocol means the device won't connect.

lessons.title: Hazardous areas in plain English
lessons.keyPoints:
A hazardous (classified) area is where flammable gas, vapor, dust or fibers could ignite. Electronics there need special protection.
In the US system (NEC): Class I = gases and vapors, Class II = combustible dusts, Class III = fibers.
Division 1 = the hazard can be present during normal operation. Division 2 = only present under abnormal conditions (like a leak).
The international system uses Zones: Zone 0, 1 and 2 for gas, from most to least likely.
Common protection methods: explosion-proof (contains an explosion inside the housing), intrinsically safe (limits energy so a spark can't ignite), and purged/pressurized enclosures.
The device must carry the right approval (for example FM, CSA, ATEX or IECEx) for the area it's going in.
Never guess. Ask: 'Is this a classified area? What class, division or zone?' Put it on the quote.
Selling the wrong approval is a safety issue, not just a return.

quiz.q: Class I areas involve:
quiz.why: Class I is flammable gases and vapors.

quiz.q: Division 1 means the hazard:
options: Can be present during normal operation
quiz.why: Division 1 is the higher-risk classification.

quiz.q: What does 'intrinsically safe' mean?
options: Energy is limited so it can't create an igniting spark
quiz.why: Intrinsic safety limits electrical energy.

quiz.q: What should go on the quote for a device in a classified area?
options: The required class/division or zone and the approval
quiz.why: Document the area classification and the approval being quoted.

lessons.title: PPE and site visit basics
lessons.keyPoints:
Every plant has its own rules. Ask your contact before the visit what PPE and training are required.
Typical PPE: hard hat, safety glasses, steel- or composite-toe boots, and hearing protection in loud areas. Keep a set in your car.
Some sites need more: flame-resistant (FR) clothing at refineries and chemical plants, H2S monitors in oil and gas, hairnets and no jewelry in food plants.
Sign in, watch the safety orientation if there is one, and stay with your escort.
Don't touch, open or adjust equipment. You're a visitor, even if you know the product.
Follow walkway markings, obey signs, and know where the exits and muster point are.
Ask before taking photos. Many plants restrict cameras.
If something looks unsafe, stop and tell your escort. Being safe is part of being professional.

quiz.q: When should you find out what PPE a plant requires?
quiz.why: Ask ahead so you show up ready.

quiz.q: A customer asks you to adjust a valve during a walkthrough. What do you do?
options: Politely decline and let their people do it
quiz.why: Visitors don't operate equipment. Their staff should.

quiz.q: Which site often requires flame-resistant (FR) clothing?
quiz.why: Refineries and many chemical plants require FR clothing.

quiz.q: What should you do before taking photos in a plant?
quiz.why: Many plants restrict photography.

lessons.title: Lockout/tagout awareness
lessons.keyPoints:
Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is how plants make sure equipment can't start or release energy while someone works on it.
Energy includes electricity, pressure in lines (liquid, gas, steam), stored spring energy, heat and chemicals.
Only trained, authorized workers apply locks and tags. As a salesperson, you're usually an 'affected' or visiting person, not an authorized one.
Never remove, bypass or operate anything with a lock or tag on it. Never.
Instruments are often removed from live lines. That's a job for the customer's trained techs, with the line isolated and depressurized.
When you recommend a product, think about safe installation: isolation valves, block-and-bleed manifolds and siphons make future maintenance safer.
In the US, LOTO is covered by OSHA's standard on the control of hazardous energy.

quiz.q: What is lockout/tagout for?
options: Stopping equipment from starting or releasing energy during work
quiz.why: LOTO controls hazardous energy during service.

quiz.q: You see a lock on a valve handle. What do you do?
options: Remove it if you need to
quiz.why: Never remove or operate anything that's locked or tagged out.

quiz.q: Which of these is a form of hazardous energy?
quiz.why: Pressurized lines store a lot of energy.

quiz.q: Which product suggestion makes future instrument maintenance safer?
options: An isolation valve or block-and-bleed manifold
quiz.why: Isolation lets techs safely remove instruments.

lessons.title: Reading a model code
lessons.keyPoints:
A model code (order code) is a string where each position or group selects an option: size, material, connection, range, output, approvals and more.
Flowmeter and transmitter codes are long because they have many options. Each character matters.
Use the manufacturer's datasheet 'ordering information' section or online configurator to build or decode a code. Don't guess.
Decode it left to right and confirm each option against the customer's application data.
Watch the easy-to-miss options: process connection size and type, wetted materials, hazardous area approval, output/communication, calibration certificate.
When replacing an existing device, get the full model code from its nameplate (a photo is best). The serial number helps the manufacturer look it up.
If a code is obsolete, the manufacturer or rep can usually give a current replacement code. Confirm the fit before quoting.

quiz.q: What does each position or group in a model code do?
options: Selects an option like size, material or output
quiz.why: Each part of the code picks a specific option.

quiz.q: Best way to get the model code for a replacement?
options: Ask for a photo of the nameplate
quiz.why: The nameplate has the exact code and serial number.

quiz.q: Where do you go to build or decode a code?
options: The datasheet ordering information or the manufacturer's configurator
Last month's invoice for a different product
quiz.why: Use the official ordering information.

quiz.q: Which option is easy to miss and causes returns?
quiz.why: Approvals, connections, materials and outputs are common misses.

lessons.title: Building a clean quote
lessons.keyPoints:
A good quote lets the customer say yes without calling you back with questions.
Include: the full model code and a plain-English description, quantity, unit price, extended price, lead time, freight terms, payment terms and how long the quote is valid.
Restate the key application data you quoted to (fluid, pressure, temperature, size, area classification). It protects you and the customer if something was wrong.
List what's included and what's not: accessories, certificates, startup or calibration.
Offer options when it helps: good/better/best, or a quick-ship alternate.
Double-check before sending: units, connection sizes, materials, approvals and quantities.
Put a follow-up date on your calendar or in the CRM the moment you send it.

quiz.q: What's the goal of a good quote?
options: Make it as short as possible
Let the customer say yes without needing to call back with questions
quiz.why: Clear, complete quotes get approved faster.

quiz.q: Why restate the application data on the quote?
options: It protects both sides if something was wrong
quiz.why: Documenting what you quoted to avoids misunderstandings.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs on every quote?
options: Lead time and how long the quote is valid
quiz.why: Lead time and validity are basic quote terms.

quiz.q: What should you do the moment you send a quote?
quiz.why: Schedule the follow-up right away so it doesn't slip.

lessons.title: Common ordering mistakes
lessons.keyPoints:
Wrong process connection: NPT size, male vs female, flange size and class, or tri-clamp size.
Wrong range: normal pressure should sit in the middle of the range, not near the top or bottom.
Wrong materials for the fluid: brass on something corrosive, or the wrong liner on a mag.
Missing approvals: hazardous area, sanitary (3-A), NACE or oxygen cleaning.
Unit mix-ups: psi vs bar, °F vs °C, gpm vs lb/hr.
Wrong output: 4-20 mA when they needed HART or Modbus.
Forgotten accessories: snubbers, siphons, manifolds, grounding rings, mounting kits.
The fix for almost all of these: confirm the application data in writing before ordering.

quiz.q: A 0-100 psi gauge on a line that runs 95 psi is an example of:
options: A wrong range: it's too close to the top
quiz.why: Normal pressure should sit near mid-scale.

quiz.q: Which is a unit mix-up?
options: Quoting bar when the customer said psi
quiz.why: psi vs bar is a classic mix-up.

quiz.q: What prevents most ordering mistakes?
options: Confirming the application data in writing before ordering
quiz.why: Written confirmation catches mistakes before they ship.

quiz.q: Which is a commonly forgotten accessory?
quiz.why: Accessories like snubbers and siphons are easy to forget.

lessons.title: Returns, RMAs and warranty
lessons.keyPoints:
Never let a customer ship something back without a Return Material Authorization (RMA) number. Unauthorized returns get lost or refused.
Get the details first: model code, serial number, PO and invoice numbers, and the reason for the return.
Anything that touched process fluid needs to be cleaned and usually needs a decontamination statement or safety data before the manufacturer will accept it.
Know the difference: a warranty claim is a product defect. A misapplication (wrong range, wrong material) usually isn't covered.
Restocking fees often apply to standard items returned for credit. Custom or configured items are often not returnable.
Be honest about what happened and what the options are. A fair, fast return builds trust.
Log the return and the root cause. If it was a quoting mistake, learn from it.

quiz.q: What must a customer have before shipping a return?
quiz.why: No RMA, no return.

quiz.q: A gauge failed because it was quoted with the wrong range. Is that usually a warranty claim?
options: No, that's a misapplication, not a product defect
quiz.why: Warranty covers defects, not application mistakes.

quiz.q: A used flowmeter that handled chemicals is being returned. What's usually required?
quiz.why: Manufacturers need to know it's safe to handle.

quiz.q: Why log the root cause of a return?
options: To learn and avoid repeat mistakes
quiz.why: Root cause tracking prevents the next return.

lessons.title: Calming an upset customer
lessons.keyPoints:
Upset customers usually want two things: to be heard, and to know what happens next.
Use LAST: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank.
Listen without interrupting. Let them finish. Take notes.
Apologize for the situation, even if it wasn't your fault: 'I'm sorry this happened. Let's fix it.'
Solve: say exactly what you'll do and when you'll get back to them. Then do it, early if you can.
Thank them for telling you. Many unhappy customers just leave without saying anything.
Don't argue, blame other departments or the manufacturer, or make promises you can't keep.
If they're abusive or it's beyond you, stay calm and bring in your manager.

quiz.q: What does LAST stand for?
quiz.why: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank.

quiz.q: What should you do while an upset customer is explaining the problem?
options: Let them finish and take notes
quiz.why: Letting them finish shows you're listening.

quiz.q: Which is a good 'Solve' statement?
options: I'll call ABB and update you by 3 pm today
Someone will get back to you
quiz.why: Specific action and a specific time builds trust.

quiz.q: What should you avoid?
quiz.why: Blaming others makes us look disorganized.

lessons.title: Keeping customers informed on late orders
lessons.keyPoints:
Bad news doesn't get better with age. Tell the customer as soon as you know an order is late.
Call for important or critical orders. Email is fine for small ones, but a call shows you care.
Give the facts: what's late, the new expected date, and why (briefly).
Offer options: partial shipment, an in-stock alternate, expediting (and any cost), or a temporary fix.
Tell them when you'll update them next, even if nothing changes. Then do it.
Ask how the delay affects them. If a plant is down, escalate right away.
Note every update in the CRM so anyone on the team can answer if the customer calls.

quiz.q: When should you tell a customer their order is late?
quiz.why: Early warning lets the customer plan.

quiz.q: Which is a helpful option for a late order?
options: Offering a partial shipment or an in-stock alternate
quiz.why: Options give the customer control.

quiz.q: A customer's plant is down waiting for the part. What do you do?
options: Escalate right away and look for any faster option
Tell them to call the manufacturer
quiz.why: Plant-down situations need urgent action.

quiz.q: Why log updates in the CRM?
options: So anyone on the team can answer if the customer calls
quiz.why: Shared notes keep the whole team informed.

lessons.title: Logging your work and following up on quotes
lessons.keyPoints:
If it's not in the CRM, it didn't happen. Log calls, visits, quotes and next steps the same day.
Good notes are short and useful: who you talked to, what they need, the application details, and the next step with a date.
Every quote gets a follow-up task the day you send it.
A simple follow-up rhythm: about 2 days after sending (did you get it, any questions?), about 1 week (where does it stand?), then about 2 weeks (decision timing?).
Every follow-up should add something: a question answered, a lead-time update, an option, or a relevant case study. Not just 'checking in.'
If you lose, ask why (price, lead time, brand, spec) and log it. Lost-quote reasons help the whole team.
Keep contacts current: titles change, people leave. Note who influences the decision, not just who buys.

quiz.q: When should you log a customer call?
options: At the end of the month
Only if it led to an order
quiz.why: Same-day notes are accurate and useful.

quiz.q: What makes a follow-up worth the customer's time?
options: Adding something useful like an answer, update or option
quiz.why: Bring value every time you reach out.

quiz.q: Why log the reason you lost a quote?
options: It helps the team spot patterns in price, lead time or brand
quiz.why: Loss reasons guide pricing, stocking and strategy.

quiz.q: When should a quote get its follow-up task?
quiz.why: Schedule follow-up immediately.

lessons.title: Forecasting honestly
lessons.keyPoints:
A forecast predicts what will actually close and when. Management uses it to plan stock, staffing and targets.
Use stages: identified need, quoted, customer reviewing, verbal yes, PO received.
Each stage has a rough likelihood. A quote just sent is far less certain than a verbal yes with a PO date.
Ask closing questions to move deals forward honestly: Who else is involved? When will you decide? What could stop this?
Update close dates when they slip. A pipeline full of old dates isn't a forecast.
Big deals deserve a plan: decision makers, competition, budget timing and next steps.
An honest forecast that's sometimes low beats an optimistic one that's always wrong.

quiz.q: What is a sales forecast for?
options: Predicting what will actually close and when
quiz.why: Forecasts help the business plan.

quiz.q: Which stage is most likely to close?
options: Verbal yes with a PO date
quiz.why: A verbal yes with a PO date is the strongest signal.

quiz.q: A deal's close date has passed with no PO. What do you do?
options: Update the date based on what the customer says
quiz.why: Keep dates honest and current.

quiz.q: Which question helps forecast accurately?
options: When will you decide, and what could stop this?
quiz.why: Knowing timing and obstacles makes the forecast real.

lessons.title: Using Claude to write follow-ups and emails
lessons.keyPoints:
AI assistants like Claude can draft emails in seconds: quote follow-ups, late-order updates, thank-you notes and meeting recaps.
Give it context: who the customer is, what you quoted, what happened, and what you want them to do next.
Example prompt: 'Write a short, friendly follow-up to Mike at the water plant about the 6 liquid-filled gauges I quoted Tuesday. Ask if he has questions and mention 2-week lead time.'
Tell it the tone and length: 'casual and under 100 words' or 'formal for a purchasing manager.'
Always read and edit before sending. Fix anything that isn't true or doesn't sound like you.
Use it to rewrite, not just write: paste a rough draft and ask it to make it clearer or more polite.
Save prompts that work well and reuse them.

quiz.q: What makes an AI-drafted email better?
options: Giving it context: who, what, and the next step you want
quiz.why: Context gives the AI what it needs to write something useful.

quiz.q: What must you do before sending an AI-drafted email?
quiz.why: You're responsible for what you send.

quiz.q: Which is a good way to use AI on your own writing?
options: Ask it to make your rough draft clearer or more polite
Let it reply to all customers automatically
quiz.why: Rewriting your own draft keeps your voice and facts.

quiz.q: How do you control tone and length?
options: Tell it, for example 'casual and under 100 words'
quiz.why: Just say what you want.

lessons.title: Account research and datasheet summaries
lessons.keyPoints:
Before a call, ask an AI to research the company's public information: what they make, their plants, recent news and likely instrument needs.
Example prompt: 'I'm visiting a dairy plant tomorrow. What instrumentation do dairies typically use, and what questions should I ask about sanitary requirements?'
Ask it to prepare discovery questions for a specific application, like steam flow or tank level.
Paste or upload a datasheet and ask for a one-paragraph summary, the key specs, and the questions to ask a customer before quoting it.
Ask it to explain a term you don't know in plain English, like 'turndown' or 'Ethernet-APL.'
AI can be wrong or out of date. Check specs against the official datasheet before you put them on a quote.
Never invent or guess specs because an AI said so. If it matters, verify it.

quiz.q: Which is a good pre-call use of AI?
options: Researching the company and preparing discovery questions
quiz.why: Prep makes your questions sharper.

quiz.q: An AI tells you a meter's accuracy spec. What do you do before quoting it?
options: Check it against the official datasheet
Put it on the quote as-is
quiz.why: AI can be wrong. Datasheets are the source of truth.

quiz.q: You upload a datasheet. What's a useful request?
options: Summarize key specs and list questions to ask before quoting
quiz.why: Summaries plus questions make you faster and better prepared.

quiz.q: What's a good way to learn an unfamiliar term?
options: Ask the AI to explain it in plain English, then confirm if it matters
quiz.why: Plain-English explanations help you learn fast.

lessons.title: AI do's and don'ts
lessons.keyPoints:
Do follow company policy on which AI tools are approved for work.
Don't paste confidential information (customer pricing, margins, contracts, personal data) into tools that aren't approved for it.
Do treat AI output as a first draft. You're responsible for anything you send or quote.
Don't let AI make technical selections on its own. Use it to prepare, then confirm with datasheets, inside sales tech support or the manufacturer.
Do use it for time-savers: emails, call prep, summaries, meeting notes and checklists.
Don't present AI-written content as verified fact without checking it.
When in doubt, ask your manager.

quiz.q: Which should you NOT paste into an unapproved AI tool?
options: A general question about vortex meters
A request to fix your grammar
quiz.why: Confidential data stays in approved tools only.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for an AI-drafted quote email?
quiz.why: You send it, so you own it.

quiz.q: Can AI choose the final product for a customer by itself?
options: No. Use it to prepare, then confirm with datasheets or tech support
quiz.why: Technical selections need verification.

quiz.q: Which is a great time-saving use of AI?
options: Drafting meeting notes and call prep
quiz.why: Drafting and prep are where AI shines.

scenarios.title: Shaking gauge at the pump
scenarios.persona: Mike, maintenance tech at a city water treatment plant
scenarios.opening: Hey, I've got pressure gauges on our high-service pump discharge that keep dying every few months. The needle shakes so bad you can't even read it. What have you got?
scenarios.hidden: Normal pressure is about 85 psi, with spikes when the pump starts. Current gauges are 2.5-inch dry brass, 0-100 psi. Mounted right on the pump discharge, outdoors. 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection. Needs 6 of them within a week.
scenarios.goodRec: A liquid-filled stainless steel gauge with a larger dial (4 or 4.5 inch), range around 0-160 or 0-200 psi so 85 psi sits near mid-scale, plus a snubber to handle the start-up spikes.

scenarios.title: Sanitary pressure on a dairy line
scenarios.persona: Karen, process engineer at a dairy
scenarios.opening: Hi, I need pressure readings on our pasteurizer line. The old gauge got flagged in an audit and I need something that'll pass.
scenarios.hidden: 1.5-inch tri-clamp connections. Normal 30 psi, max 60 psi. CIP cleaning with hot caustic around 180 F. 3-A sanitary required. Would like a 4-20 mA signal to the PLC eventually. Food-grade fill if any fill fluid is used.
scenarios.goodRec: A sanitary 3-A diaphragm seal with tri-clamp connection and food-grade fill, on a gauge or a sanitary pressure transmitter with 4-20 mA. Range around 0-60 or 0-100 psi.

scenarios.title: Steam flow for cost allocation
scenarios.persona: Raj, utilities engineer at a chemical plant
scenarios.opening: I need to start measuring the steam going to one of our process units so we can charge it back to them. The old orifice plate on that line is shot.
scenarios.hidden: 4-inch line. Saturated steam at about 150 psig. Flow from 2,000 to 10,000 lb per hour. DCS takes 4-20 mA with HART. Would prefer less permanent pressure loss than the orifice.
scenarios.goodRec: A vortex flowmeter, ideally with built-in pressure or temperature compensation to output mass flow, or a multivariable DP setup. Confirm the turndown covers 2,000 to 10,000 lb/hr.

scenarios.title: Tank level with foam
scenarios.persona: Dana, operations lead at a chemical blending plant
scenarios.opening: Our level transmitter on one of the mixing tanks goes crazy every time the agitator kicks on. I need something that actually works.
scenarios.hidden: Current unit is ultrasonic. 12-foot tank. Heavy foam and solvent vapor when mixing. Class I Division 2 area. Needs 4-20 mA. Also wants a separate high-level alarm because they overflowed once.
scenarios.goodRec: Guided wave radar (or high-frequency non-contact radar) with the right hazardous-area approval, plus an independent point level switch such as a vibrating fork for the high-level alarm.

scenarios.title: Sour gas compressor gauges
scenarios.persona: Travis, field supervisor at a natural gas compressor station
scenarios.opening: I need to replace a bunch of pressure gauges on our compressor lines. Can you quote me something?
scenarios.hidden: Gas contains H2S, so NACE MR0175 materials are required. Normal pressure about 1,200 psi. Strong vibration from the compressors. Outdoors in heat and cold. Company requires safety-pattern gauges (solid front, blowout back) above 1,000 psi.
scenarios.goodRec: NACE-compliant wetted parts (stainless or Monel), liquid-filled safety-pattern gauge, range about 0-2,000 or 0-3,000 psi, plus a snubber.

scenarios.title: Oxygen service gauges
scenarios.persona: Angela, purchasing agent at an industrial gas filling plant
scenarios.opening: I need gauges for our oxygen cylinder filling station. Our last supplier shipped the wrong ones and I can't have that again.
scenarios.hidden: Cylinders fill to about 2,200 psi. Gauges must be cleaned for oxygen service and marked 'Use No Oil'. Needs cleaning certification paperwork. Quantity 20.
scenarios.goodRec: Gauges cleaned and certified for oxygen service, marked 'Use No Oil', safety-pattern construction, range around 0-4,000 psi, with cleaning certification included.

scenarios.title: Replace a broken gauge
scenarios.persona: Linda, maintenance tech at a packaging plant
scenarios.opening: Hi, the gauge on our air compressor line got knocked and the glass cracked. Can I get a replacement?
scenarios.hidden: It's on the compressed air line, which runs about 100 psi. The face says 0 to 160 psi. It's a 2.5-inch dial with a 1/4-inch NPT connection on the bottom. She needs 2.
scenarios.goodRec: A 2.5-inch dry pressure gauge, 0-160 psi, 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection, quantity 2: the same as the one that broke.

scenarios.title: Reorder what we bought last time
scenarios.persona: Tom, buyer at a chemical plant
scenarios.opening: Hey, we bought some gauges from you a while back and I need more of the same ones.
scenarios.hidden: He has the part number from the old order or the tag on the gauge (he'll read it off if asked). He needs 10. He needs them by the end of the month. Ship to the same plant address as before.
scenarios.goodRec: Get the part number (or old PO) to match the exact item, confirm quantity 10 and the end-of-month need date, then send a quote for the same part.

scenarios.title: Gauge needle near the top
scenarios.persona: Carlos, operator at a water plant
scenarios.opening: Hi, the needle on one of our gauges is always sitting near the top. It's hard to read and I'm worried it's going to break.
scenarios.hidden: The gauge is 0-100 psi but the line normally runs about 90 psi, and can go up to 110. It's a 4-inch dial with a 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection. He needs 1.
scenarios.goodRec: A 4-inch gauge with a higher range, 0-200 psi, so 90 psi sits near the middle of the dial; same 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection, quantity 1.

scenarios.title: Dry or liquid-filled?
scenarios.persona: Beth, maintenance tech at a bakery
scenarios.opening: Quick question. What's the difference between a dry gauge and a liquid-filled one? I need a gauge for a pump.
scenarios.hidden: The gauge goes on a pump that shakes quite a bit. Normal pressure is about 60 psi. Current gauge is 2.5-inch with a 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection. She needs 3.
scenarios.goodRec: Explain that liquid fill calms the needle and protects the gauge from shaking, then recommend a 2.5-inch liquid-filled gauge, 0-100 psi, 1/4-inch NPT bottom connection, quantity 3.

scenarios.title: Thermometer for a hot water tank
scenarios.persona: James, facilities tech at a manufacturing plant
scenarios.opening: I need a dial thermometer for one of our hot water tanks. Can you help?
scenarios.hidden: The water runs about 150 F. The opening in the tank is 1/2-inch NPT. He needs about a 6-inch stem to reach into the water. He needs 1.
scenarios.goodRec: A bimetal dial thermometer, 0-250 F range, 6-inch stem, 1/2-inch NPT connection, quantity 1. Bonus: suggest a thermowell so it can be removed without draining the tank.

scenarios.title: When to change the air filters
scenarios.persona: Maria, facilities manager at an office building
scenarios.opening: We keep forgetting to change the air filters on our air handlers. Is there a gauge that tells us when they're dirty?
scenarios.hidden: It's for the air filters on the building's air handlers. The pressure is very low, about 0.5 to 1 inch of water column across the filter. She needs 4, one per air handler.
scenarios.goodRec: A Dwyer Magnehelic differential pressure gauge, 0-2 inches of water column, mounted across each filter, quantity 4. When the reading climbs, it's time to change the filter.

scenarios.title: Replace an old magmeter
scenarios.persona: Dave, operator at a wastewater plant
scenarios.opening: Hi, our old flowmeter on the return line died. Can you help me replace it?
scenarios.hidden: It's a mag meter on wastewater. 6-inch line with flanged connections. It sends a 4-20 mA signal to the plant control system. He needs 1. It's not a hazardous area.
scenarios.goodRec: An ABB ProcessMaster (or ABB water mag) 6-inch flanged magmeter with a liner suited for wastewater and 4-20 mA output, quantity 1.

scenarios.title: Track compressed air use
scenarios.persona: Sarah, maintenance planner at a plastics plant
scenarios.opening: We think we're wasting a lot of compressed air. Is there a way to measure how much we're using?
scenarios.hidden: It's the main compressed air header, a 3-inch line. It runs about 100 psi. She wants to see usage on the plant system with a 4-20 mA signal. She needs 1 to start.
scenarios.goodRec: An ABB SensyMaster FMT430 thermal mass flowmeter for the 3-inch air header with 4-20 mA output, quantity 1. It reads low flows well, so she can see leaks when the plant is idle.

scenarios.title: Win the steam meter from the other brand
scenarios.persona: Greg, utilities engineer at a paper mill who has always used another brand of vortex meter
scenarios.opening: We've always used the other guys' vortex meters. I need a new steam meter on a line with barely any straight pipe. Why would I look at ABB?
scenarios.hidden: 6-inch saturated steam line at about 125 psig. The only meter spot is about 4 pipe diameters after an elbow. The other brand's quote required re-piping for straight run, which means a shutdown. He wants lb/hr into the DCS with HART. He's budget-sensitive. Decision in about 3 weeks, and the plant manager has to approve anything over budget.
scenarios.goodRec: ABB SwirlMaster FSS430 (or FSS450 if they want energy) in 6-inch with the integrated temperature sensor for saturated steam mass flow and HART. Sell the avoided re-piping and shutdown cost, confirm the straight-run requirement from the installation guide, and respect the incumbent instead of knocking it.

scenarios.title: Defend Coriolis on price
scenarios.persona: Priya, purchasing manager at a specialty chemical plant
scenarios.opening: Your Coriolis quote is almost twice what we pay for the turbine meters we use now. Why should I pay that?
scenarios.hidden: They batch a solvent (not conductive) into reactors on 2-inch lines. The turbine meters wear and need recalibration about every 6 months. Batches are often off-spec, which wastes product. The lab checks density separately on every batch. Operations wants fewer meter failures. The process engineer, Tom, is part of the decision.
scenarios.goodRec: ABB CoriolisMaster FCB430 or FCB450, 2-inch, with batching (FillMass). Sell total cost: no moving parts to wear, VeriMass verification in place instead of pulling meters, in-line density that can cut lab checks, and less product giveaway. Ask what an off-spec batch costs, and bring the process engineer into the conversation.

scenarios.title: Replace the orifice plate on fuel gas
scenarios.persona: Marcus, energy manager at a food processing plant
scenarios.opening: We've got an old orifice plate measuring natural gas to our boilers and nobody trusts the numbers. What would you do?
scenarios.hidden: 4-inch natural gas line at about 5 psig. Flow swings from very low at night to high in the morning, and the orifice reads poorly at low flow. The impulse lines clog and have frozen in winter. He wants gas use per boiler to prove energy savings. He needs 4-20 mA plus a totalizer. There are 2 boilers.
scenarios.goodRec: ABB SensyMaster FMT430 or FMT450 thermal mass meters, 4-inch, one per boiler (quantity 2). Direct mass flow, wide turndown for the low night flows, very low pressure loss, and no impulse lines to clog or freeze, with 4-20 mA and a built-in totalizer.

specs.title: Batching vegetable oil
specs.application: A food plant wants to batch vegetable oil accurately into mixing tanks. 2-inch stainless line, room temperature, about 20 gpm. They want high accuracy and a 4-20 mA output to the batch controller.
specs.why: Oil isn't conductive, so a mag meter won't work. Coriolis measures mass directly with high accuracy, which is ideal for batching.

specs.title: Cleanroom filter monitoring
specs.application: A pharma plant needs a local gauge showing pressure drop across HVAC filters for a cleanroom. The drop runs from about 0.2 to 0.8 inches of water column. No signal needed, just a reading for the daily walk-through.
options: Low-range differential pressure gauge, such as a Dwyer Magnehelic, 0-1 in. w.c.
specs.why: Filter loading is a very low differential pressure in inches of water. A low-range DP gauge like the Magnehelic is built for exactly this.

specs.title: Furnace temperature at 1,800 F
specs.application: A heat-treating furnace runs at about 1,800 F (around 980 C). The customer needs a temperature signal to the controller and wants the sensor to be replaceable without shutting down.
options: Pt100 RTD in the open air
Thermocouple in a protection tube or thermowell
specs.why: At 1,800 F you're past the range of standard RTDs. A thermocouple in a protective well handles the heat and can be replaced without shutdown.

specs.title: Abrasive slurry pump discharge
specs.application: A plant pumps a thick, abrasive slurry. Standard gauges plug up within weeks and the readings freeze. Pressure is about 60 psi. They need a local reading.
options: Standard brass gauge with a snubber
Gauge with a diaphragm seal, such as an inline (flow-through) seal
specs.why: Solids clog the gauge socket. A diaphragm seal keeps the slurry out of the gauge, and an inline seal is self-cleaning in the flow.

specs.title: Throttling cooling water
specs.application: A customer wants to automatically control cooling water flow to a heat exchanger to hold a process temperature. The plant has instrument air and the DCS outputs 4-20 mA.
options: Globe control valve with a pneumatic actuator and positioner
Ball valve with a manual lever
specs.why: Precise throttling calls for a globe control valve. Pneumatic actuation uses their instrument air, and the positioner follows the 4-20 mA signal.

specs.title: Temporary flow check without shutdown
specs.application: A wastewater plant wants to check pump flow on a 10-inch line for a few weeks to settle a performance dispute. The line can't be shut down or cut.
specs.why: Clamp-on ultrasonic straps onto the outside of the pipe, so no cutting or shutdown is needed. It's ideal for temporary checks.

specs.title: Steam meter right after an elbow
specs.application: A chemical plant needs to measure saturated steam to a reboiler on a 4-inch line. The only place for the meter is about 4 pipe diameters after an elbow, and re-piping would mean a shutdown. They want steam mass flow in lb/hr with 4-20 mA and HART.
options: ABB SwirlMaster FSS430 with the integrated temperature sensor
specs.why: SwirlMaster needs only about 3 diameters in and 1 out after an elbow, and with the built-in RTD it calculates saturated steam mass flow. A standard vortex needs much more straight run. Mags can't measure steam, and thermal mass meters are for gases, not steam.

specs.title: Water main in a vault with no power
specs.application: A water utility wants to measure flow on an 8-inch water main inside an underground vault. There's no power at the site. They want the data for billing and to spot leaks.
options: ABB AquaMaster electromagnetic flowmeter (battery or solar powered)
specs.why: AquaMaster is built for water distribution, billing and leak detection, and can run on battery or solar power where there's no electricity.

specs.title: Abrasive lime slurry
specs.application: A treatment plant doses lime slurry through a 3-inch line. The slurry is abrasive and has worn out their last meter. They need 4-20 mA with HART to the control system.
options: ABB ProcessMaster magmeter with an abrasion-resistant liner
ABB Totalflow µFLO G5 flow computer
specs.why: Slurry is conductive, so a mag meter works, and its open bore has no moving parts to wear. The key is choosing an abrasion-resistant liner and suitable electrodes. Vortex meters don't suit slurries, and thermal meters are for gas.

specs.title: Natural gas to a boiler burner
specs.application: A food plant wants to control the fuel-to-air ratio on a boiler. They need mass flow of natural gas on a 4-inch line at about 5 psig, with very little pressure loss, plus 4-20 mA to the burner controls.
specs.why: SensyMaster measures gas mass flow directly with no pressure or temperature compensation and very low pressure loss, which suits low-pressure fuel gas. Mags only measure conductive liquids.

specs.title: Batching syrup and checking Brix
specs.application: A beverage plant batches sugar syrup into mixing tanks. They need accurate mass for each batch and want to see sugar concentration (Brix) in-line instead of sampling in the lab. Sanitary tri-clamp connections are required.
specs.why: The hygienic FCH400 measures mass flow and density, and DensiMass converts density to concentration like Brix. A mag measures volume only and can't give concentration.

specs.title: Gas well sales measurement
specs.application: A producer measures natural gas sales at a remote wellsite with an orifice meter. There's no utility power. They need volumes calculated to AGA standards and data sent back to their SCADA system.
options: ABB Totalflow µFLO G5 flow computer with solar charging
specs.why: The µFLO G5 is a single-run gas flow computer with a built-in DP, static pressure and temperature sensor, AGA calculations, and battery/solar power for remote sites.

specs.title: What else would you quote? Steam energy
specs.application: A customer is ordering a VortexMaster FSV430 for superheated steam. Now they mention they want to bill steam energy to each department. What's the most important change or add-on to suggest?
options: Upgrade to FSV450 and add an ABB 266 pressure transmitter for the pressure input
specs.why: Superheated steam energy needs pressure and temperature. The FSV450 can take an external pressure signal and calculate mass and energy, and a 266 transmitter supplies that pressure.

specs.title: What else would you quote? Mag on plastic pipe
specs.application: A customer is buying a mag meter for a PVC line that feeds a control valve. They also mention the valve 'hunts' and never settles, and it has an old pneumatic positioner. What should you add to the quote?
options: Grounding rings for the mag, and an ABB TZIDC digital positioner for the valve
specs.why: Mags on plastic or lined pipe need grounding rings to read accurately. A hunting valve with an old positioner is a classic upgrade for a digital positioner like the TZIDC.
